sections.history: Sivapuri lies a few kilometres from Chidambaram in the Chola country north of the Kaveri. In the Tevaram the place is called Tirunelvayil, the gateway of the paddy fields, a name that recalls the fresh rice lands that once surrounded it. Sambandar sang ten verses in praise of the Lord here, and the temple is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams. Accounts say the saint came to worship every day during his stay in Chidambaram, and the shrine has been remembered for that devotion ever since. The temple that stands today is a structural building of the medieval Tamil period, enlarged by later patrons, and it has stayed in continuous worship. It lies close to its neighbour, the Palvannanathar temple at Tirukkazhippalai, so the two Tevaram shrines are often visited together.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a three-tiered rajagopuram, set within concentric rectangular walls. The sanctum holds Uchinathar in the form of a small, self-manifested linga, and behind it are images of Shiva and Parvati together, a quiet reminder of the story of the place. The goddess Kanakambikai is honoured in her own shrine. Within the enclosure the sacred tank, known as Krupa Samudram, lies close at hand, and the trees held sacred here are named as the gooseberry and the bamboo. The proportions are modest, in the manner of the old village shrines of the Chola country, and the stonework is plain rather than showy.
sections.legends: The name of the Lord of Midday comes from the saint Sambandar. Travelling with his devotees and relatives, the child-saint grew weary and hungry as the sun stood overhead, and the party had no food at hand. Shiva, it is said, took the form of a temple priest and fed them all in the heat of the day, then vanished, leaving the company to realise whose hospitality they had received. From this the Lord is called Uchinathar, the Lord of Noon (uchi, midday), and in Sanskrit Madhyaneeswarar. Another tradition tells that the sage Agastya was granted a vision of the wedding of Shiva and Parvati at this place. Sources differ on small details of the meal story, so it is best received as a tradition of the shrine, a tale of the Lord who feeds the hungry devotee.
sections.festivals: Vaikasi Visakam, in the Tamil month of Vaikasi (May or June), is named as the most prominent festival of the temple. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Sivapuri is best visited as a short, unhurried stop beside Chidambaram. Come under the eastern gopuram, pass through to the sanctum of Uchinathar, and look for the small linga with Shiva and Parvati behind it, then visit Kanakambikai in her own shrine. Devotees remember the Lord here as the one who fed the hungry, and it is a gentle place to pray for daily bread and a household that never goes without. Nearby is the tank, and the neighbouring Tirukkazhippalai temple is only a short walk away, which makes a pleasant morning of two Tevaram shrines. The temple is quiet, and the air in the courtyard is that of a small village sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Sivapuri lies a few kilometres south-east of Chidambaram, close to the Annamalai University campus, and is easily reached from Chidambaram by auto-rickshaw or local bus. Chidambaram has the nearest railway station and bus stand. The Tirukkazhippalai Palvannanathar temple is only a few hundred metres away on foot. Puducherry and Chennai are the nearest airports, both several hours away by road.
